name: Gravitational Potential Energy
what: This subtopic covers gravitational potential energy changes in uniform fields using Eg = mgΔh, qualitative understanding of potential energy changes in non-uniform fields, and how to determine changes in gravitational potential energy from the area under force–distance and field–distance graphs.
why: Gravitational potential energy is central to energy conservation problems involving masses moving in gravitational fields. The graphical method is particularly important for objects travelling large distances where the uniform field approximation no longer holds.

items.title: I can calculate gravitational potential energy change in a uniform field using Eg = mgΔh
items.what: In a uniform gravitational field, the change in gravitational potential energy is Eg = mgΔh, where m is the mass in kg, g is the gravitational field strength in N kg⁻¹, and Δh is the change in height in metres.
items.why: This formula applies to any situation where the gravitational field can be treated as uniform — typically within a few hundred metres of a planet's surface — and is the standard method for energy calculations in projectile and motion problems.
items.example: A land diver of mass 60 kg jumps from a platform 30 m above the ground on Pentecost Island. His change in gravitational potential energy is Eg = 60 × 9.8 × 30 = 17 640 J, which is converted to kinetic energy during the fall.

items.title: I can explain why Eg = mgΔh cannot be used for large changes in height
items.what: The formula Eg = mgΔh assumes g is constant throughout the motion. As an object moves large distances away from Earth, g decreases significantly according to the inverse square law, making the constant-g assumption invalid.
items.why: Using Eg = mgΔh for large distances (such as launching a rocket to orbit) would give a significant underestimate of the energy required, because it fails to account for how gravity weakens with distance.
items.example: At Earth's surface, g ≈ 9.8 N kg⁻¹. At the altitude of the International Space Station (408 km), g ≈ 8.67 N kg⁻¹. For a rocket travelling to 10 Earth radii, g changes by a factor of 100, so Eg = mgΔh would be far too inaccurate.

items.title: I can determine the change in gravitational potential energy from the area under a force–distance graph
items.what: The change in gravitational potential energy equals the work done against gravity, which is represented by the area under a gravitational force–distance graph. For non-uniform fields, this area is estimated by counting squares on the graph.
items.why: This graphical method is the required technique for calculating potential energy changes when a mass moves through a non-uniform field, such as a spacecraft travelling to high altitude.
items.example: A force–distance graph shows a spacecraft experiencing a force decreasing from 6000 N near Earth's surface to near zero at great distance. Counting approximately 13 squares, each representing 3 × 10⁹ J, gives a total ΔEg ≈ 3.9 × 10¹⁰ J.

items.title: I can determine the change in gravitational potential energy from the area under a field–distance graph multiplied by mass
items.what: The change in gravitational potential energy can also be found by multiplying the area under a gravitational field strength–distance graph by the mass of the object. The area under the field–distance graph has units of N kg⁻¹ × m = J kg⁻¹, and multiplying by mass (kg) gives joules.
items.why: Field–distance graphs are independent of the mass of the object moving through the field, making them more versatile than force–distance graphs. The same graph can be used to find ΔEg for any mass placed in that field.
items.example: A field–distance graph for Earth shows an area of approximately 2.5 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹ between two orbital heights. For a 1200 kg space telescope, ΔEg = 2.5 × 10⁷ × 1200 = 3.0 × 10¹⁰ J.

items.title: I can qualitatively describe how gravitational potential energy changes as a mass moves in a gravitational field
items.what: Gravitational potential energy increases as a mass moves away from the centre of a gravitational body (against the direction of the field) and decreases as the mass moves toward the body (in the direction of the field). In a radial non-uniform field, potential energy increases at a decreasing rate as distance increases.
items.why: A qualitative understanding of potential energy changes is useful for reasoning about satellite motion, orbital transfers, and the energy requirements for space travel without needing detailed calculations.
items.example: A spacecraft moving from low Earth orbit to a higher geostationary orbit gains gravitational potential energy. As it continues further from Earth, the rate at which it gains potential energy decreases because the gravitational force weakens.
